# Haggle Canva speaker notes

Deck: https://canva.link/hja6pu0hyq4ziq1
Target: 2 minutes 30 seconds, including brief pauses. Approximately 350 spoken words. Source annotations are not spoken.
Canva MCP exposes read-only presenter notes, no notes-writing or animation operation. These notes have not been inserted into Canva. No animation was applied.

## 1 — 00:00–00:12 — Haggle
We built Haggle, an autonomous procurement negotiator. It reads the supplier, proposes binding offers, and closes the deal. The goal is the best whole deal, including payment terms and risk.

Source: docs/design.md. Autonomous operation demonstrated in practice and offline runs, not a production procurement deployment.

## 2 — 00:12–00:30 — Simulated value
Across our audited ten-case practice suite, negotiated total cost was 1.17 million euros below the opening offers. That is a 9.16 percent reduction. The arena values payment terms and penalties as well as price. These are simulated costs, not actual business savings.

Source: presentation/ANALYSIS.md:22 and presentation/src/evidence.json. C_open = EUR 12,759,510.63; C_deal = EUR 11,591,349.12; difference EUR 1,168,161.51. Benchmark started 11 October 2026, 01:44 UTC, code c4fb3d5, gpt-6.1-sol, built-in prompt SHA 45be8588d0. Later partial batches do not supersede this complete benchmark.

## 3 — 00:30–00:52 — Binding numbers
Our key engineering decision: code owns the binding numbers. It calculates facts, prices the allowed packages, checks constraints, and decides when to close. The model interprets the supplier and writes the email. It can select from the offer menu, but it cannot invent a binding price.

Source: docs/design.md and presentation/ANALYSIS.md:16. Avoid claiming every retained package is exactly equal-cost: strategy analysis documents security packages above the target. Numeric email validation and checked fact markers support this boundary; no claim of formal verification.

## 4 — 00:52–01:12 — Higher price, better deal
Here is why that matters. In one practice case, 432 euros with 90-day payment beat 427 euros with 14-day payment on modeled total cost. The higher sticker price bought more time to pay. A price-only negotiator would prefer the worse package.

Source: docs/haggle-evidence.md, P03 structure-retention row; docs/haggle-strategy-analysis.md:32. Exact displayed unit prices EUR 432.15 and EUR 427.49. Historical observed comparison, not a matched causal experiment. Do not use the older narration's 65.9 to 73.5 score claim: that describes P02, not this P03 comparison.

## 5 — 01:12–01:27 — Ten-case benchmark
That complete suite closed all ten cases, satisfied every must-have, and averaged 77.22 percent on the arena score. This is one hosted practice run per case. It is neither a leaderboard best-of score nor a hosted final result.

Source: docs/haggle-strategy-analysis.md:7–28. All 114 recorded HTTP responses were 200, no model errors or decision fallbacks. Morning changes after this version have not been validated by this benchmark.

## 6 — 01:27–01:43 — Measured progress
Three complete runs on the same practice cases moved from 65.25 to 77.22 percent. We changed policies between runs, so this is descriptive progress. It does not prove which change caused the gain, or guarantee the same result on unseen cases.

Source: presentation/ANALYSIS.md:31–36, evidence.json. 10 October 19:54 and 20:20 UTC, 11 October 01:44 UTC. Same model gpt-6.1-sol. No controlled or replicated causal claim.

## 7 — 01:43–02:00 — What suppliers count
One useful failure: a new fact ID was not always a new argument. Suppliers verified forty claims, but treated eleven as duplicates. None were contradicted or irrelevant in that suite. We learned to track the argument's meaning, rather than simply attach another record.

Source: docs/haggle-strategy-analysis.md:36–39; docs/haggle-bug-list.md B3. Counts exclude closing confirmations. These counts support duplication insight, not a controlled evidence-versus-pressure comparison. Morning deduplication fixes have narrow hosted checks, not proven full-suite score gains.

## 8 — 02:00–02:20 — Failure rehearsal
Then we broke every model call. In an offline rehearsal across fifty cases, forty-five ended in deals and five took the alternative. None remained unresolved. The economics and fallback runner still completed the work. That tests failure handling locally. It does not establish hosted final performance.

Source: docs/handoffs/2026-10-11-0030-final-readiness.md:23 and :37; HANDOVER.md. probes/final_rehearsal.py --llm broken --cap 120, five waves, exit 0, self-stop in 11.4 minutes. Offline scripted simulator, distinct from hosted practice.

## 9 — 02:20–02:30 — Close
Haggle turns supplier conversations into checked, binding offers. Our takeaway is concrete: give the model the conversation, give code the economics, and optimize the whole deal.

Evidence boundary: no hosted-final result or real-world savings is claimed. No claim about current rank, commit counts, archive size, or fixed-price acceptance.

   105	{"action": "send" | "settle", "subject": "...", "body": "...e-mail text with [[cN]] markers...",
   106	 "offers": ["A", "C"], "rationale": "one or two sentences: what you read in their reply and why these packages"}"""

   108	
   109	def group(claim):
   110	    """The kind the arena counts once per supplier: a second claim of a group comes back `duplicate` ("already taken
   111	    into account") and buys nothing. Across ~1,300 replies: quality notifications after a scorecard claim 59/59
   112	    duplicate (30/30 verified without one), a scorecard after quality notifications 12/12, a second scorecard span
   113	    8/8, a second forecast of the same part 21 of 28.
   114	    Index falls count per series. Each new rival offer is new data (P05: "took it into account" every round), so
   115	    rival offers have no group."""
   116	    kind = claim.get("kind")
   117	    if kind == "rival offer":
   118	        return None
   119	    if kind in ("delivery", "quality", "complaints"):
   120	        return "performance"
   121	    if kind in ("index", "forecast"):  # per series / per part: a bundle's parts are separate arguments (API brief)
   122	        return kind + ":" + claim["refs"][0].split("@")[0]

   127	    """The model's answer broke a rule; the message goes back to it as a correction."""

   134	    try:

   159	                "no index clause"

   162	                f"{v['deadband_pct']}% deadband, base {v['base_month']})"
   163	            )
   164	        else:
   165	            out.append(f"{k}={v}")

   167	
   168

   170	
   171	
   172	def _num(figure):
   173	    digits = re.sub(r"[^\d.,-]", "", figure).replace(",", "")
   174	    try:

   176	    except ValueError:
   177	        return None

   179	
   180	def unverified_figures(body, allowed):

   182	    backs: written by the model itself, they are unchecked (an arena `contradicted` costs trust)."""
   183	    ok = {_num(f) for f in FIGURE.findall(allowed)} | {_num(x) for x in re.findall(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)?", allowed)}

   186	
   187	def _struct(terms):
   188	    return repr(sorted((k, repr(v)) for k, v in terms.items() if k != "unit_price"))

   191	def _place_sentence(before, text):

   197	    return text

    The haggler scored 30.6 on the practice board with half the hosted

      behaviour, no case-specific rules; claims ranked by strength;
      unverified figures in the e-mail are sent back; fixed terms are named

      P01, P02, P05, P08
    - RFQ: one gate per session, focus on the two cheapest bidders,
      case-wide spent IDs, rival offers cited, case-wide target, immediate
      close on the cheapest settled bidder, re-read a thread whose sheet a

content.text:
Four concrete lessons **actually present in the built-in system prompt**:

| Jury slide title | Exact prompt quote | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **“Your opening offer can become your ceiling.”** | “Every package we send binds us.” | `simulation/starter-kit/arena_kit/haggle/agent.py:49` — introduced by `d28e7c7` |
| **“Find their currency. Trade in it.”** | “They tell you their currency.” | `agent.py:61`; cash, security and contract examples at `:76–79` |
| **“When price stops moving, change the deal.”** | “Each kind of case has its natural lever.” | `agent.py:66–71` — case-specific *types*, introduced by `20f2c17` |
| **“Persuasion gets checked before it gets sent.”** | “Facts and figures only through the claim markers” | `agent.py:93–97` — introduced by `d28e7c7`; runtime numeric validator at `:180–184` |

The second is especially memorable: longer payment, index protection or contract security can mean more to the supplier than their modeled cost to us. Present it as an insight encoded in the prompt, not a universal law.

**Important distinction:** “argument families count once” is primarily **runtime enforcement**, not an explicit general rule in `SYSTEM`. The prompt says “Never repeat one” at `:58`; semantic grouping lives at `:109–123`, and duplicate-family feedback at `:664–668`. Safe wording: **“We taught the agent—and enforced in code—that another fact ID isn’t another argument.”**

Effective-prompt route: `settings.py:89–93` uses the built-in `SYSTEM` when the custom file lacks the `"offers"` schema. Archived benchmark logs confirm that route; do not call the obsolete custom draft the active prompt.

Avoid quoting the prompt’s “every package costs us the same” as an invariant: later strategy analysis documents retained security packages above target.
